content: Platelet-rich therapies are increasingly being utilized in the management of musculoskeletal soft tissue injuries, including ligament, muscle, and tendon tears, as well as tendinopathies. These therapies can serve as either the primary treatment or as an adjunctive procedure, such as being applied after surgical repair or reconstruction. The process involves centrifuging a sample of the patient’s own blood to isolate the platelet-rich fraction, which is then applied to the injured tissue, often via injection. Platelets are known to release various growth factors, which theoretically promote tissue healing. However, it remains necessary to evaluate whether these biological effects translate into meaningful clinical benefits. The objective of this study was to assess the benefits and potential harms of platelet-rich therapies in treating musculoskeletal soft tissue injuries. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Bone, Joint and Muscle Trauma Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and LILACS, covering studies up to March 2013. Additional searches included trial registries and conference abstracts. No restrictions were placed on language or publication type. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials comparing platelet-rich therapy with placebo, autologous whole blood, dry needling, or no platelet-rich therapy in patients with acute or chronic musculoskeletal soft tissue injuries. The primary outcomes assessed were functional status, pain, and adverse effects. Data extraction and risk of bias assessment were performed independently by two reviewers, with disagreements resolved through discussion or arbitration. Statistical analyses included risk ratios for dichotomous data and mean differences or standardized mean differences for continuous data, with 95% confidence intervals. The quality of evidence for each outcome was evaluated using GRADE criteria. The review included 19 small, single-center trials (17 randomized and 2 quasi-randomized) involving a total of 1,088 participants. These trials addressed eight clinical conditions: rotator cuff tears (arthroscopic repair), shoulder impingement syndrome surgery, elbow epicondylitis, anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction, ACL donor graft site application, patellar tendinopathy, Achilles tendinopathy, and acute Achilles rupture surgical repair. The trials were further categorized into two groups: those where platelet-rich therapy was the primary treatment (five trials) and those where it was used as a surgical augmentation procedure (14 trials). Most participants were male, except in studies involving rotator cuff tears and elbow or Achilles tendinopathies. Only three trials were judged to have a low risk of bias, while the remaining 16 were at high or unclear risk due to issues such as selection bias, detection bias, attrition bias, or selective reporting. The methods for preparing platelet-rich plasma (PRP) varied significantly across studies, with no standardization or quantification of the PRP applied to patients. Data for the primary outcomes—function, pain, and adverse events—were pooled from a maximum of 11 trials, representing 45% of the participants. The evidence for all primary outcomes was rated as very low quality. Short-term functional outcomes (up to three months) were assessed in four trials involving three clinical conditions, using four different measurement tools. These results showed no significant difference between platelet-rich therapy and control groups (SMD 0.26; 95% CI -0.19 to 0.71; P = 0.26; I² = 51%; 162 participants). Medium-term functional outcomes (at six months) were evaluated in five trials across five clinical conditions, again showing no difference between groups (SMD -0.09; 95% CI -0.56 to 0.39; P = 0.72; I² = 50%; 151 participants). Long-term functional outcomes (at one year) were pooled from 10 trials involving five clinical conditions, with no significant differences observed (SMD 0.25; 95% CI -0.07 to 0.57; P = 0.12; I² = 66%; 484 participants). While the confidence intervals suggested the possibility of either poorer outcomes in the platelet-rich therapy group or moderate benefits, these differences were not clinically meaningful. Pain outcomes were assessed in four trials involving three clinical conditions. A small reduction in short-term pain was observed in favor of platelet-rich therapy on a 10-point scale (MD -0.95; 95% CI -1.41 to -0.48; I² = 0%; 175 participants). However, the clinical significance of this finding was marginal. Adverse events were reported in four trials, while seven trials reported no adverse events. There was no significant difference in the number of participants experiencing adverse effects between the treatment and control groups (7/241 vs. 5/245; RR 1.31; 95% CI 0.48 to 3.59; I² = 0%; 486 participants). For individual conditions, pooled data from six trials assessing long-term function after platelet-rich therapy application during rotator cuff tear surgery showed no statistically or clinically significant differences between groups (324 participants). Overall, the available evidence is insufficient to determine whether platelet-rich therapy has meaningful effects on individual clinical conditions. In conclusion, there is currently insufficient evidence to support the routine use of platelet-rich therapy for treating musculoskeletal soft tissue injuries. Researchers planning future randomized controlled trials should consider the scope of ongoing studies and address the need for standardization in PRP preparation methods.
